subsubtopic: ARMS LIMITATION TALKS BETWEEN UNITED STATES AND RUSSIA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Considering that Canada is playing a greater role in the present U.S. space shuttle program than ever before, notably in terms of hardware, experimental devices and scientific personnel; and considering that the strongest impetus toward an increased U.S. presence in space is the escalating strategic arms race, including the planned deployment of high-energy killer lasers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Win-nipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That the Canadian government urge the U.S. Senate and the Reagan administration to press for further arms limitation talks with the Soviets so that the space program is not dominated by military planning which threatens to plunge the U.S. into a strategic space war with the Soviet Union.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under Standing Order 43.
In light of the tragic and brutal massacre of 30 Salvadorans on April 7 by right wing forces, and in light of Canada's support of the United Nations' resolution of December 15 last condemning El Salvador's human rights record and requesting the United Nations Commission on Human Rights to examine the situation in El Salvador, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That this House convey to the El Salvadoran representatives in Ottawa our deep shock and outrage over the senseless killings of April 7, and urge the United Nations Human Rights Commission to commence its investigation into human rights violations in El Salvador forthwith so that further tragedies of this sort may be deterred through international pressure.

subsubtopic: IMPACT ON BUSINESS AND EMPLOYMENT IN ALBERTA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43

subsubtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF YUKON CAPITAL TRUST FUND-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has stated publicly the government's anticipation that the Yukon may be given provincial status by 1985. The need for revenues from non-renewable resources by a province for the

installation of needed infrastructure is vital. Therefore, to accumulate such capital, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen):
That the government immediately establish a Yukon capital trust fund and direct into it all royalties from current oil, natural gas and mineral production in the Yukon. And furthermore, that the fund be used exclusively for capital works and infrastructure construction in the Yukon, and that, pending provincial status, the fund be administered jointly by the national and Yukon territorial governments.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing order 43. Whereas the Big-stone Indian Band in northeast Alberta is nearing the completion of its protest march for economic equality in which both young and old band members are demonstrating their desperate need for economic assistance by walking 400 kilometres to gain the attention of the government, and whereas the band has received no indication from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), or the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. de Bane) that the government intends to address the very serious poverty and unemployment that plague these people, despite the fact that the government's western development fund was supposed to have placed the needs of native people in the west at the top of its priority list, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger):
That this House condemn the government for its lack of response and compassion in this case, and demand that the government act immediately by meeting with the band so that a comprehensive plan may be developed to assist the band members to begin the arduous task of raising their standard of living and attaining economic independence.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, perhaps the Prime Minister would care to familiarize the House with the government's policy concerning one related matter, that is, the question of foreign investment. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the assertion that some foreign investment is not too welcome is a policy followed by many governments, including the government which preceded mine, mine and probably the one which will follow mine.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to confirm that after a series of meetings between parliamentary leaders and consultations with our respective caucuses it would appear that the House may now be informed of a special order which is likely to get unanimous agreement. I simply want to take this opportunity to thank the parliamentary leaders of the other
April 8, 1981

parties who have been patient and who, in spite of the climate in the House, have always shown willingness to attend the meetings which were necessary to reach this agreement. Therefore, Madam Speaker, I will read the full text which in a few minutes might prove to be the solution and the way to end the constitutional debate, should the House agree unanimously.

That the motion of the Minister of Justice for an Address to Her Majesty concerning the Constitution of Canada, Government Orders, Government Business, No. 36, shall be disposed of as follows:
1.	The motion and any amendments proposed thereto shall be the business considered on Tuesday, April 21, 1981, Wednesday, April 22, 1981, and Thursday, April 23, 1981, and on those days no member shall speak for more than thirty minutes.
2.	No later than 6:00 p.m. on April 21, 1981 the House leader of the Progressive Conservative Party and the House leader of the New Democratic Party, and no later than 10:00 p.m., on April 21, 1981, the government House leader may give notice of one amendment to the said motion affecting one or more provisions of the motion and any such amendments shall be printed on the notice paper until disposed of.
3.	No amendments or subamendments may be proposed to the said motion except as provided in the preceding paragraph.
4.	At 9.45 p.m. on April 23, 1981, the Speaker shall put without further debate or amendment every question necessary to dispose of any proposed amendment and any amendment put on notice pursuant to paragraph No. 2 of this order which shall be deemed to have been proposed for the purpose of this order. No member shall rise to speak after this hour, but all such questions as must be decided in order to comply with this order shall be decided forthwith before the House adjourns.
5.	The government shall not designate any days on which the said motion shall be dealt with until the first sitting day following the rendering of the decision by the Supreme Court of Canada on the appeals concerning the opinions of the Manitoba Court of Appeal rendered on February 3, 1981, and the Newfoundland Court of Appeal rendered on March 31, 1981 on the questions put to the said courts concerning the amendment of the Constitution of Canada.
6.	On any day that is designated for dealing with the said motion as may have been amended, the hours of sitting shall be as follows:
On Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays: From 10.00 a.m. to 1.00 p.m. and from 2.00 p.m. to 11.59 p.m.
On Wednesdays: From 2.00 p.m. to 11.59 p.m.
On Fridays: From 11.00 a.m. to 1.00 p.m. and from 2.00 p.m. to 7.00 p.m.
Provided that on any such day no private members' business or proceeding pursuant to Standing Order 40 shall be taken up.
6(a) A designated day for the purposes of this order is a day appointed by a minister of the Crown by written notice to the Clerk at least twenty-four hours in advance and, if necessary, such notice shall be published in a special notice paper. A day shall be deemed a designated day for the purpose of this order regardless of whatever proceedings are before the House at any time during that day.
7.	On any day designated by the government pursuant to the preceding paragraph no member shall speak for more than twenty minutes and no amendments shall be proposed.
8.	At fifteen minutes before the time of adjournment on the second day designated by the government pursuant to the paragraph numbered 6 and 6(a) of this order the Speaker shall at that hour put the motion as may have been amended. No member shall rise to speak for any purpose after that time and all questions necessary to dispose of the said motion of the Minister of Justice shall be put forthwith without further debate.
Provided that nothing in this order shall be considered to affect in any manner or to any degree the separation of the legislative and judicial powers, a fundamental principle of our Constitution.
Business of the House
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to join the government House leader in this matter. I think what we have accomplished by the negotiations which he described embodies four things. We have provided an opportunity for the federal-provincial process to work in the traditional way. The proposal really says this is nothing more than a special order of the House to govern its conduct of the debate which will follow. It permits all parties a reasonable opportunity for access to the amendment process. It permits the House to have the benefit of the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada and to take it into account in the debate which will ensue thereafter.
We are agreed with the proposition put by the government House leader, and we are prepared to consent.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me particular pleasure to join with the other two House leaders in submitting to this House of Commons this historic agreement. The time that it has taken to arrive at this document has been very lengthy. We have had many meetings. I am sure there is not any aspect of the whole matter that we have not discussed, but it has been worth it because, as I say, we have achieved an agreement which I believe will prove to be historic.
As should happen in all bargaining sessions, each of us gave something, each of us won something. We are particularly pleased that we now have the guarantee that our amendments concerning aboriginal rights and equal status between men and women will come before the House for a vote. One other thing that we are pleased about, of course, will be shared by all members of the House. That is that we will be permitted to enjoy life without the trauma of closure.
When this debate is over after five more days of debate, however it comes out, whatever the vote is on the final motion, it will be the people of Canada who will have scored the greatest gain, for our Parliament will have acted in a civilized manner. That is the way we should act. 1 dread the thought of what the scene would have been had we not reached an agreement. We should act in a civilized manner and we shall now do so. In that way Parliament will have the right to be proud of what it will have done. We give our unanimous support to this agreement.

Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rose on a point of order yesterday having to do with the proper treatment of the judiciary in this honourable House by members of the House. In particular, I refer to Hansard for Monday, April 6. The Prime Minister, in replying to a question by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble), as reported at the top of page 8988, said this:
Madam Speaker, it is basic to our system that three judges, five judges, or nine judges, cannot tell us what is right. We are elected by the people. We are answerable to the people-
It is the job of the courts to judge whether these laws are intra vires or ultra vires.
With that I agree.
What the opposition has been doing is saying "We are timid fellows-"

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext:
-"because three non-elected officials have told us that such a thing could not be done."
With those remarks the Prime Minister was referring to the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal of Newfoundland, Chief Justice Mifflin, and to Mr. Justice Morgan and Mr. Justice Gushue of the Court of Appeal of Newfoundland. He referred to them as three non-elected officials. These are three appointed members of the judiciary, and it is so important that this House always remember that they are to be kept completely independent and treated in this House with the respect the judiciary should be accorded. I will refer to Beauchesne on that point in moment.
They are not non-elected officials; they are non-elected members of the courts of this land and, in the case of Newfoundland, of the highest court of that province. Chief Justice Mifflin was appointed in 1964 by the Pearson administration, Mr. Justice Morgan was appointed in May, 1975, by the administration of the present Prime Minister, and Mr. Justice Gushue was appointed in February, 1976, by the administration now headed by the Prime Minister.
As if that were not enough, this slighting and insulting reference to three non-elected officials who have told us that such a thing could not be done-this is the historic decision rendered March 31 by the Newfoundland Supreme Court which held that it was beyond the constitutional jurisdiction of this Parliament to pass certain resolutions-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Order. The hon. member must recognize that a point of order has to be short. If I understand the point of order the hon. member is trying to make, and I have before me the statement made by the Prime Minister, to which the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) is objecting, he should state quite simply why he feels these words were unparliamentary, that would suffice. I would ask him not to discuss the substance of what took place in the Supreme Court of Newfoundland; that is not relevant to the point of order. We should keep this fairly short, and by that I mean a few sentences will suffice to make a point of order.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I now wish to make reference to another page of Hansard on the same subject. I intend to be very short, Madam Speaker. This is a matter of the dignity and independence of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland, and there I do not intend to be too short.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: In Hansard of Tuesday, April 7-

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite are not going to bully me, the Supreme Court of Newfoundland or the Supreme Court of Canada. As reported at page 9027 of Hansard for Tuesday, April 7, the Prime Minister carried on in the same manner as the day before. In reply to a question from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), he said, referring to the opposition and the premiers:
If they want to fight the fight politically, they are saying what we have been saying for the past 12 months, it is a political issue, and that they have only used the courts to subvert the courts to their own political means.
April 8, 1981

If that means anything, it is an allegation that the province of Newfoundland in particular-because the only appeal court that has held against the government's constitutional proposals so far is the Supreme Court of Newfoundland-has used the courts in Newfoundland, or is subverting the courts in Newfoundland, to its own political means. That is an allegation that the judiciary in Newfoundland is not independent, that it has somehow been subverted by the province to their cause, that it has not acted judicially and with independence and reason. It is an allegation that it has somehow been subverted to their own political means by the provinces, in this instance by the province of Newfoundland.
Let me give the authority from Beauchesne so that hon. members opposite will not think this point of order is entirely frivolous. I refer to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fifth edition, page 103:
Besides the prohibitions contained in S.O. 35, it has been sanctioned by usage that a Member, while speaking, must not:-
(h) cast reflections upon the conduct of judges of superior courts, unless such conduct is based upon a substantive motion;
These are judges of a superior court in Newfoundland, the Supreme Court of Newfoundland on appeal.
At page 114 in the section headed "Protected Persons", paragraph 321 of Beauchesne provides:
(1) All references to judges and courts of justice of the nature of personal attack and censure have always been considered unparliamentary, and the Speaker has always treated them as breaches of order.
That is why I have risen on a point of order. Hon. members have been interrupted in Committee of the Whole by the chairman when they have cast an imputation upon a judicial proceeding. In this case, there have been imputations cast upon a judicial proceeding, unless the Prime Minister wants to clearly withdraw the statement which he made, or clarify it, and there have been imputations cast with respect to the three judges of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland, all of whom were appointed by the government opposite and its predecessor. All of those judges are impeccable. Chief Justice Miffin has a record of 17 years of unparalleled service in Newfoundland. He is very highly regarded by the Bar and in no way should he be held up to ridicule in this House as a non-elected official. He has been a judge since 1964. He was appointed Chief Justice of the trial division in July of 1975 by the government of the Prime Minister, and in December of 1979 he was made Chief Justice of the Newfoundland Court of Appeal by the administration of the Leader of the Opposition.
This is a course of action started by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), whose job in this House is to protect the judiciary and who said on October 6 last that he was opposed to going to the Supreme Court of Canada because-and I quote from The Globe and Mail-"The Supreme Court is very unreliable and timing is very important".
I would like the Prime Minister to clarify whether he will say, once the justices of the Supreme Court of Canada have ruled, that they have been subverted in some way or other by
Point of Order-Mr. Crosbie
the provinces or by the hon. members of the opposition if the decision is not in accord with the decision that he wants, or if they affirm the decision of the Newfoundland Court of Appeal. Are they to fear a public attack from the Prime Minister if they do their duty in the appeal which they will be hearing on April 28? They are not in a position to defend themselves in the political arena. It is for the hon. members of this House to see that the judges are protected and not attacked or have slurs cast on them in this House by the Prime Minister, who is the first among us. The Prime Minister is the man-or the woman-who gives us the lead, the example. He is in no way superior to me. He is the first minister, but he is not one whit better than I am in this House, nor in my view is he one whit better than I am outside of the House.
However, I would ask the Prime Minister, before the Chair rules-and I know this was said during the question period in the heat of being questioned on a matter in which he is very much interested-to withdraw any suggestion that the judges of the Newfoundland Supreme Court are simply non-elected officials, or that anyone has subverted them. Because the word "subvert" means to overturn them, to upset them, to effect their destruction or to overthrow them. That is the definition in The Concise Oxford Dictionary.
The Prime Minister has said that the judges of the Newfoundland Supreme Court have had their destruction effected by the provinces, that they have been overthrown, overturned or upset. It is the Prime Minister who is upset and overturned and overthrown by this judgment, not the other way round.
I am not going to get excited about this. I have put this matter calmly before you, Madam Speaker, and I ask the Prime Minister to clear away this very unfair attempt to denigrate the Newfoundland Supreme Court.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the short answer would be that I have never heard such nonsense from a man who pretends to be equal to other hon. members in this House. However, I will give a longer answer to that.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Yes, you had better!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Now I am being threatened by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie).

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Well, your own reputation would demand it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext:
My first point is that I referred to the judges as non-elected officials. Madam Speaker, we both agree that they are non-elected. As to whether they are officials, I looked up the definition in The Concise Oxford Dictionary and I found the word "official", when used as a noun, meant "presiding officer or judge of archbishop's, bishop's, or especially archdeacon's court; person holding public office". So we know that one can be a judge of one kind and be called an official. An official is also a person who holds office. One reads in the same dictionary that "office" is defined as "position with

April 8, 1981
Point of Order-Mr. Crosbie
duties, to wit, attached to it, place of authority or trust or service, especially of a public kind".
If anyone would be insulted because one is called a public official, it seems to me one must be even more thin-skinned than the hon. member for St. John's West. It is obvious-

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Really humorous. It is very humorous.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: It is obvious that I was using the expression "non-elected official" as opposed to the expression of "elected official", and we in this House are elected. I do not consider it an insult to myself to be called an elected official.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Never been described as that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: I am there to serve the public of Canada. When I was making the distinction between elected and non-elected, I was really-

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: It is not like sophism.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: What are you wondering about over there?

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: "Sophism", he says it is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Do you mean "sophistry", or "paralogism"? Which do you mean? It cannot be both. It has to be one or the other. I think the hon. member is really referring to paralogism, but it is not paralogism, if he will listen to my argument. I am sorry that the hon. member for St. John's West is wasting our time by raising such a spurious point of order or point of privilege.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: You think so?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext:
The division of powers is what I had in mind. It is accepted, in the very House order that we have all just agreed upon, that there is a fundamental distinction between the executive, the legislative and the judicial function. In this case, I was making the distinction between those who are elected officials and therefore part of the legislative power, and judicial officials who are part of the judicial power; they must be separate. So much for the suspicion that I might be accusing some people of something, debasing them by calling them non-elected officials.
The second argument was really a sophistic one, namely, that by accusing the provinces of subverting the courts, or using the courts to their political advantage, somehow-

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Not "using", "subverting".

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: -that is an attack on the courts. If the hon. member is suggesting that I might be attacking the provinces, then he might have a point; but to say that I am attacking the courts because I am saying that someone else is trying to use them is obviously sophistry.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: You are saying they allowed themselves to be used.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Will the hon. member stand and say where I said they allowed themselves to be used? Will he stand up and say that right away?

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: The Prime Minister said that it is a political issue and they have used the courts to subvert the courts to their own political means. That means that the courts-

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: -have allowed themselves to be used and subverted. That is plain English. It is saying that the courts are not independent and have allowed themselves to be so used.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: My case stands, Madam Speaker. The hon. member has just proved the point that he is talking nonsense.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-REFERENCE BY MR. TRUDEAU TO NEWFOUNDLAND SUPREME COURT JUSTICES
speechtext:
I have the two texts of Hansard dated April 6 and 7, to which the hon. member for St. John's West has referred and about which he has raised a point of order. The first one to which he had reference is on April 6. He felt that the reference to the judges of the Supreme Court as being non-elected officials could be denigrating or insulting to these officials. That was the only direct reference that the Right Hon. Prime Minister made to the judges. The fact that the reference was to the effect that they were non-elected officials does not seem to be either denigrating or insulting.
In my understanding of the other text, the Right Hon. Prime Minister did not speak of the courts but of the premiers, and he expressed an opinion on the way in which the premiers might be conducting their political battle in the case that concerns us. In the course of describing that situation, the Right Hon. Prime Minister used the word "subvert". The hon. member for St. John's West read the Oxford Dictionary, as I did, and he has given us the definition of "subvert", which is, of course, not an unparliamentary expression. On that ground I have to say that the point of order of the hon. member for St. John's West is not well taken.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order to seek the instructions of the Chair with regard to a notice which I gave the Chair about a week ago respecting the provisions in the main estimates of the current fiscal year, 1981-82, which I believe to be out of order based on rulings by Your Honour and previous Speakers.
I seek clarification by the Chair as to when this matter might be proceeded with. It obviously would be most advantageous to the smooth conduct of business if it were proceeded with at a time when the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) could be present. Tomorrow or the next day would be satisfactory.
After looking through the history of this matter over the last ten years, I believe this is the first occasion on which this type of point has been raised with regard to the main estimates.
April 8, 1981

Heretofore it has always been with respect to the supplementary estimates, which provide a rather limited supply period, and therefore it was seen to be appropriate, near the end of the supply period but prior to the appropriations act being presented to the House, that this point of order be raised.
I suggest to the Chair that it might be beneficial to the smooth conduct of business both here in the House and in the committees which are currently hearing these main estimates if this matter might be examined now. If the Chair were able to find that the votes which I will bring to the Chair's attention are in fact out of order, then I think it would be conducive to the smooth conduct of government business and House business here and in the committees to have the matter brought to the attention of the House at an early rather than late date.
To put it simply, I suppose I am asking direction from the Chair as to whether tomorrow or the next day, if it suits the agenda of the President of the Treasury Board, I might raise the details of the points of order with respect to those items in the main estimates.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have received notice of the hon. member's intention to raise a point of order on this particular point, and I thank him for having given me that notice.	.
I just want to point out to the hon. member that those estimates constitute an order of reference for the committees and they cannot be discussed in the House until they have been reported by the committees. If the hon. member is seeking some remedies, it is perhaps through the committees that he might seek them.
However, this does not preclude the hon. member from raising a point of order at the time when the estimates will be reported to the House or deemed to have been reported to the House. It has been helpful when those points of order have been raised somewhat in advance of the time when the estimates have been discussed in the House, and I think closer to the date, that is, May 31, on which the estimates are to be reported or deemed reported to the House, I would entertain the hon. member's point of order. I think I would like to delay the matter until we get closer to that date, if that is agreeable to the hon. member. I think we will then be in a better position to deal with that problem.

Madam Speaker, I do not have any particular reason for concern, other than the fact that committees are now studying the votes, many of which I humbly submit are out of order; but if there is no problem with the committees studying votes which will subsequently be deemed out of order, there is no problem as far as I am concerned.
I do not wish my remarks to be taken as criticism, but one of the characteristics of previous decisions by the Chair is that when the Chair has concurred in the fact that certain votes were out of order, your Honour's predecessors have taken the position: "In view of the fact that we have just now known about it, we will leave them here, but let this be warning that this should not happen in the future". By virtue of the Chair's leniency in the past with regard to this type of thing and leaving in appropriations bills items which the Chair had
Privilege-Mr. Shields
judged were out of order-but given the time were left in-we now have circumstances in which those basically illegal votes are being used again in another illegal fashion. We have a perpetuation. I would not like the matter to be left so long that we would be back into the same circumstance of saying, "Well, given the time and so forth we will leave them in this time and hope the government will bear in mind the decision of the Chair", because, as I hope to point out when discussing the main estimates, that has not turned out to be the case in some instances.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think I understand the hon. gentleman's intervention. It seems that we are having some trouble determining which of those votes are in order and which are not. With respect to discussions which might take place between the different interested parties, it seems that those parties always agree on the principles, but when it comes down to the actual votes, there is disagreement as to which ones are in order and which ones are not. It seems that what the Chair is doing as these estimates come back to the House is determining as we go along which of the votes the Chair feels are in order.
I do not think votes have come back because of the leniency of the Chair. I think everyone is trying to define which of the votes are in order and which are not in order. That is the reason my predecessors asked if these points or order concerning this particular matter could not be brought earlier rather than later. I will entertain points of order to try to determine which of the votes are in order, but closer to the day on which the estimates will be reported back to the House. I think that is the difficulty. As we go along we have to reflect on each and every one of those votes.
I was going to suggest that at some point there be a meeting between the interested parties, but it seems they all agree when they meet. It is when the actual estimates come out that there is disagreement. So I suppose it is the responsibility of the Chair to determine by the different rulings which of the votes are in order and which are not. I will do that, and I will be more than grateful if the hon. member gives me the wisdom of his opinion.

STATUS OF CLAUSE IN BILL C-57
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope to be commendably brief on a matter which breaches my privilege as a member of the House and of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. It arises out of the committee's present study of Bill C-57, which is the budget bill giving effect to the proposals on the Excise Tax Act, the Excise Act, and on a revenue tax in respect of petroleum and gas.
I am referring in particular to paragraphs 25.12 and 25.13 at page 53 of the bill. The Chair may have received judicial notice of a judgment of the Court of Appeal of the province of Alberta dated March 20, 1981, declaring that the purported attempt by Her Majesty in right of Canada to tax natural gas, the property of Her Majesty in right of the province of Alberta, was ultra vires the power of the Government of Canada. Yesterday, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) confirmed that he was not amending Bill C-57, that he had not yet made up his mind, along with his colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) to appeal this judgment, and therefore the judgment that that portion of the act is ultra vires the powers of the Government of Canada is annulled. By a House order, this bill will be reported back to the House no later than Wednesday, April 15. In the interval, there are still a few witnesses to be heard tomorrow, and then the committee will consider the bill clause by clause.
My question of privilege is that I am put under the obligation of voting yea or nay on a clause which is being ruled illegal. It is not enough, I submit to you, Madam Speaker, to say that an hon. member can vote against it. That is only a Marie Antoinette type of remedy because there is no alternative, no choice. In fact, this clause is only part of an omnibus bill. If I find it repugnant to my position as a Member of Parliament, whose responsibility it is to uphold the law, to insist on voting against this clause, I must vote not only against sections 25.12 and 25.13, but I must vote against the whole of Clause 43 of the bill, which is Part II of the bill, and, in fact, against the whole bill, even though I may approve of a great deal of it.
My question of privilege is simply that the Minister of Finance has refused to remove that particular section and therefore not only members of the committee but all of us find ourselves in this position. Ultimately, unless there is an appeal carried to the Supreme Court of Canada which would reverse the judgment of the Court of Appeal of Alberta, or unless the minister amends this bill, we will have to vote for something that is illegal, unless we vote the bill down and defeat the government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATUS OF CLAUSE IN BILL C-57
speechtext:
Again the hon. member is raising a question of privilege similar to the ones which have been raised in the House on a resolution. What the hon. member has just said leads me to conclude that he would like me to confirm the
April 8, 1981

judgment of the court declaring that clause in the bill ultra vires. I cannot do that. The hon. member knows that the Speaker should not make such a judgment. As a matter of fact, the rules governing the Speaker in the House of Commons enjoin the Speaker not to do that.

As a Member of Parliament, it is his responsibility to determine on what side of the question he wants to vote. Therefore, I do not see that he has a legitimate question of privilege, and certainly he has not established a prima facie case.

speechtext:
Perhaps with that request I will state specifically to what my question of privilege refers. It refers to statements in Hansard of October 17, 1979, at page 303 an earlier ruling by yourself, and at page 8787 and 8790 of Hansard of last Tuesday. My problem relates to interjections and how interjections in the House of Commons are handled, particularly when there might be conflict among the various levels of recording in the House as to where the priority should lie. This is a very important matter to me. This particular interjection has given rise to my question and I think in fact will make the case that it needs further consideration by Madam Speaker.
My question of privilege is twofold, and it relates in part to recorded remarks made by members in Hansard. The second part arises out of the remarks themselves. As to the first part, the remarks were made last Tuesday during an exchange in question period between the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien). The Minister
Privilege-Mr. Wenman
of Justice was just finishing his answer, and his final remarks were as follows:
Of course, the Prime Minister said, and it is the position of the government, that we respect the decision of the courts. But we will finish our duty as Members of Parliament to finish the work that we have started in the fall, and of course we will wait for the decision of the Supreme Court before deciding to press the matter in England-yes or no.
At that point the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made an interjection which I heard or thought I heard at the time. The interjection seemed to say, in effect, "anything if we can get it out of the House".
I wanted to be absolutely certain that in fact the Prime Minister had made the remark, so I checked with the videotape at the broadcasting unit the next morning. The videotape in fact confirmed that the Prime Minister had made a remark to this effect. To be doubly sure, I checked the blues, and to my surprise the Prime Minister's remarks were not recorded. When Hansard arrived at my office at 12 noon the next day, I discovered the remarks were not recorded there either. I must confess I find the omission extremely disturbing, as I would like to show in the second part of my argument.
Apart from the omission, which was puzzling in itself, if hon. members would refer to pages 8787 and 8790 of Tuesday's Hansard, they will notice that there are a large number of interjections which were faithfully recorded. It is in fact the faithfulness and the detail to which our Hansard reporters went that make it even more amazing that this particular remark, which was possibly one of the more significant remarks of the day, was not included.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. WENMAN-OMISSION OF INTERJECTION FROM OFFICIAL REPORT
speechtext:
Order, please. If I understand, the hon. member is telling me that Hansard has not properly recorded all the things he himself heard from his seat, and that subsequently he listened to the tapes and found those particular interjections.
I will not entertain the hon. member's arguments any longer because that, in itself, is not a question of privilege. I want to tell him that Hansard is not a verbatim report of what happens in the House, and some would say "thank God it is not". At any rate, it is not a verbatim report; it is as complete a report as possible of what has taken place in the House of Commons.
We do everything we can to make that report as complete as possible. When interjections are not heard by the reporters and are not so recorded, there is not much the Chair can do about it; possibly the Chair itself did not hear those interjections. At any rate, this does not constitute a question of privilege. The point of the hon. member is well taken, but if Hansard reporters have not reported the interjections, then they are not part of the record and that is final.
The hon. member is not seeking the floor to comment upon my decision, is he?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order relating to the question of privilege which I raised in a letter to you dated April 1, 1981. In that letter I gave you notice of a question of privilege which was quite different in kind and character from the other questions of privilege which you first considered on that day and on subsequent days. Basically the question of privilege related to what I considered and perceived to be the preferential treatment given to Members of Parliament in relation to their access to the Official Report of the House of Commons, commonly known as Hansard. I think I gave you details of the question of privilege in the letter.
I do not want to prolong the matter here; I am quite willing to submit to you, Madam Speaker, a substantial memorandum on the subject. I have done some research and have tried to determine what was the origin of this practice of giving such
preferential treatment, and I want very briefly to mention three points.
First, in a memorandum dated March 27, 1981, Madam Speaker referred to the practice of granting access to Hansard and indicated that ministers, former ministers, parliamentary secretaries and others were given special and preferential treatment in relation to the examination of the transcript of the Hansard report, that other members had to obtain access to Hansard in a different way.
Second, I want to point out that on October 17, 1979, as reported at page 303 of Hansard for that day, Mr. Speaker Jerome stated that the Speaker is in charge of Hansard, exercises control over it and is responsible for the proceedings.
Third, I want to point out that the Senate and House of Commons Act and other legislation make it very clear that members of the House are Commoners; they share the privileges of this House in common. Indeed, on April 1, in response to a question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), Madam Speaker underlined again the equality of members of this House.
I cite all those points in support of my question of privilege. As I say, I do not want to prolong the matter in the House. I realize there are differences of opinion, even among members on this side of the House, about the matter, but 1 think I can demonstrate very clearly that we, as members of the House, ought to receive the same privileges in respect of the services of the House of Commons. Outside and off Parliament Hill we may not expect to receive equality of treatment; but if we do not receive it in the House with respect to the privileges and services provided by the House under the jurisdiction of Madam Speaker, then I think the privileges not only of myself but of all those who are victimized by this preferential treatment are dishonoured.

subsubtopic: STUDY OF WAGE RATES IN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SECTORS
speechtext: Has the government considered the creation of a neutral body which would examine the comparability of wage rates in the private and public sectors and, if so, would such a body have the responsibility for suggesting rate changes prior to the negotiation of new collective agreements?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: STUDY OF WAGE RATES IN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SECTORS
speechtext:
There exists presently an agency within the Public Service Staff Relations Board, the pay research bureau, whose role is to obtain information on rates of pay, employee earnings, conditions of employment and related practices prevailing both inside and outside the public service to meet the needs of the parties to bargaining.
The needs of the employer and the bargaining units are established, by the pay research bureau, under the aegis of an advisory committee on pay research, comprising representatives of Public Service of Canada employers and certified bargaining agents, in order that the bureau's programs reflect their needs as closely as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we offered amendments to this Post Office bill in committee, some of which were accepted and others refused. The clause by clause consideration of the bill in committee was speeded up so that it could be reported to the House prior to the Christmas adjournment. As a result, some of the matters before the committee were not given proper consideration, even though it sat till eleven o'clock one night. Some of the amendments which were not considered in committee are now before us.
After the Christmas adjournment, the House returned in early January. At that time we were given the assurance that we would deal immediately with this urgent legislation, but presumably between then and now it lost some of its urgency and is now treated by the government as filler legislation. Nevertheless, we take this bill very seriously. That is the reason the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) brought forward this motion, which specifically directs the publication of the salaries of people appointed as vicepresidents. Under clause 10 of the bill the board has the right to fix the salary of such number of vice-presidents as it considers necessary.
The object of this motion is to ensure that those salaries shall not exceed the scale fixed by the governor in council. In other words, we would not approve the appointment of a number of vice-presidents whose salary is determined without public knowledge. The bill provides that directors of the corporation are to be appointed by the minister of the Crown and the governor in council responsible for the corporation. It is only proper and right that the salary of that appointment should be fixed. There is no reason for the remark made by the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) last evening that the salaries of these officers would be hidden.
Motions Nos. 6 and 7 which stand in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) and myself, which are grouped for voting purposes, are similar in that they call for the direction of the governor in council to be published in The Canada Gazette. The point of these motions is to ensure that the public can see what is happening. We think that is important.
I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian public is very unhappy with the way in which the Post Office is operating at the present time under the direction of this minister. Indeed, the same is true of the situation under previous ministers. The minister has claimed that the Post Office works to 95 per cent efficiency. A letter sent by the Inspector General of Banks from Place Bell Canada to my office in the Centre Block took only seven days! I sent that information to the Postmaster General. This morning I received a letter from the Minister of health in the province of Ontario asking me to get together with him about the task force committee on inter-provincial financial relations. That letter took eight days to come from Toronto. If the minister regards that as good delivery, then he is quite right, because that is 95 per cent of the type of delivery we get and expect.
April 8, 1981

Mr. Speaker, we are not going to accept the appointment of vice-presidents without knowing the types of persons being hired and their salaries. Considering the experience we have had with this organization in the past, why should we allow the salaries of the chief executive officers to be kept from the public?
Last night the minister claimed that the corporation should have an element of independence. That is a laudable idea but it should not be entirely an independent organization. The minister does not claim that the organization is in competition with any other. Indeed, the whole tenor of the bill is to give the Post Office a monopoly on the delivery of letters. It is not a question of trying to protect the post office against competitors or of not allowing those competitors to know the internal workings and salaries of the executive officers of the Post Office. If it is not in competition with other companies or organizations, what is wrong with disclosure? Where is the competitive disadvantage that disclosure, or lack of it, would give the Post Office?
This bill is an attempt to establish a new corporation which will restore public confidence in the Post Office. The minister will not accept my colleague's amendment because he wants to hide something. This is not the way to build confidence in or a new sense of direction for this corporation. Surely the minister must go to the public and the House of Commons openly and say that all the cards will be laid on the table, disclosing who will be appointed vice-president and what salary will be paid. That is the kind of openness we want and we think that is necessary if this corporation is to be a success.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed that the hon. member for Wellington-Duff-erin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) did not take the opportunity to come to the committee to put forward this amendment. I think he has some concerns that he worries about.
However, I would like to respond to some of the comments made by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn). We are not talking about whether salaries will be hidden; the amendment provides that we fix the salaries. Members of this party want to see the best representatives possible sitting on the board of directors.
We have some serious problems in the Post Office. We want that board to be able to select individuals who will represent the people of Canada. When that is done, the board will be presented to the governor in council for approval. We accept that. That kind of process was referred to in the committee. We accept the wording of the bill and, therefore, we oppose the amendment.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a few pertinent remarks specifically to the proposed amendment before the House. I listened with some interest to the comments made by the last speaker. Believe me, it would certainly be my intention, and I am sure the intention of all hon. members, that we have vice-presidents and other officers
Canada Post Corporation Act
of this intended Crown corporation who are competent and efficient and can inject some semblance of business judgment into the functioning of what otherwise has been a lacklustre and incompetent government department. However, that is an entirely different story, one which would take a great deal more time than the 20 minutes accorded me with respect to this matter. As I have indicated, I do not intend to take that long.
Let me deal with the provisions of the bill presented to us and the suggested amendments which have been made by our party. Clause 10(2) as it presently stands reads:
The board may, with the approval of the governor in council, appoint and fix the salary of such number of vice-presidents as it considers necessary.
On first reading one might come to the conclusion that it was intended that not only should the governor in council fix the number, but it should also fix the salary. I submit that on a strict legal interpretation of the words as they appear, that requirement of governor in council approval would be satisfied in the event that the corporation through its board, approached the governor in council and asked: "Will you grant to us the right to fix the salary and appoint the number of vice-presidents that we choose?" The governor in council would reply "Yes". Thereby the requirements of the subclause would have been met.
What we are concerned about is not whether we have efficient service-that is an entirely different matter-but whether at any time anyone but this corporation shall determine how many vice-presidents it has and how much they are paid.
In this bill we will be embarking upon a system foreign to Parliament, I submit. Yesterday I mentioned my views with respect to the laws, specifically regulations, affecting the public in Canada which this corporation may pass, and which, if breached, could result in fines or imprisonment of Canadian citizens.
We now have the board of this corporation entitled as of right to appoint 10,000 vice-presidents and pay them $1 million each, should the board so choose, without so much as the right to determine the number of vice-presidents or their salaries, I am not saying by Parliament, but at least by the governor in council. Surely the government at this stage is not fearful of the fact that it should exercise rights which a government is normally prepared to undertake and discharge.
If we examine the amendment, it simply has the effect of dividing up and removing any interpretation difficulty which currently exists, so that clause 10(2) would read:
The board may appoint and fix the salary of such number of vice-presidents as it considers necessary.
The board would have that authority, subject to what we propose by way of the addition of subclause (3) to clause 10, which provides:
The salaries fixed by the board pursuant to subsection (2) shall not exceed such amount as may be prescribed by the governor in council for the Corporation.

April 8, 1981
Canada Post Corporation Act
That necessary amendment, I submit, is both logical and reasonable. I recommend it to the Postmaster General in the event that he can direct some attention to this matter. I recommend it also to our colleagues on the other side of the House. I hope all members of this House would take seriously the recommendations made by other members of this House who desire to serve the public and whose interest it is to see that taxpayers' dollars currently spent on this project, or postage revenue generated by this corporation, will be astutely administered. It is only prudent and reasonable that we should have some regard for the scrutiny that the government should give to determining the maximum salaries paid to vice-presidents of this intended corporation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate for a few minutes in the debate on this amendment. I listened last night to the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker). What we are debating is the formation of a monopoly. The hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke suggested that if the monopoly were to face a situation where it was no longer a monopoly but would have competition, the competition would then skim off the cream. In other words, all the profitable parts of the service would be skimmed off, and the Crown corporation would be left to deliver the unprofitable parts. I suppose that is a natural tendency.
I could agree with his proposal if the Post Office today would at least deliver the cream, but it does not. When it takes three weeks to deliver a letter from Toronto to Vancouver-or as someone has said, a penny a day is not bad-one wonders whether the Post Office is willing to deliver the cream.
One of the most important features we should incorporate into the operation of a monopoly is the process of scrutiny, to make sure that the monopoly is operating in the best interests of the public it is supposed to serve. I think the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke would agree with that. We must ensure that the public is protected from the callousness which is an inherent trait of human nature and is part of a monopolistic enterprise. I suggest we need an arm's length relationship to government by way of a commission to control this kind of monopoly. We have it in the telephone systems of Canada whereby the government by legislation creates a monopoly because it is the best way to deliver service to the Canadian people. If the cable systems of Canada are going to be a monopoly and the subscribers are going to be either the recipients or the victims of that monopoly, they deserve some protection from government by the creation of a commission to protect the subscribers.
Today a citizen goes to the post office and buys a stamp for 17 cents. The only assurance he has when buying that 17-cent stamp is that it will cost another 17 cents to deliver the letter. It actually costs 34 cents to deliver a letter. We have no guarantee of service.
Is the Crown corporation now being formed going to ensure that service is important? Will we have the same system of
priorizing the delivery of mail that we now have in the Vancouver post office, the distribution centre for British Columbia? First-class local mail receives first treatment, followed by provincial or national mail and then by international mail. During rush periods the international mail is piled up. It is set aside until such time as the rush is over. Then it is delivered. People wonder why it takes three, four or Five weeks for a letter from the U.K. to be delivered to a household in British Columbia. They do not realize that most of that time has been spent in storage in the post office in B.C.
Will there be a provision in the legislation that there be a regulatory commission which will ensure that the subscriber will receive maximum service from this Crown corporation?
The second trait that is inherent in human nature as it applies to a monopoly is that a monopoly tends to grow. With growth it tends to become inefficient. That is why I submit the amendment we are now debating is very intelligent and apropos to this Crown corporation.
I suggest the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke look at the experience of B.C. Hydro and see what has happened to that octopus over the past 20 years since it became a Crown corporation. He will see how much it has grown with seemingly very little checks against the kind of growth it has had. Would it not be circumspect in protecting the consumer that there be a built-in mechanism to ensure there are checks against unrestrained growth of this corporation? The board of directors should be limited as to the number of directors they can appoint. There should be no nepotism, no inflating of salaries. Limits should be set on salaries.
As the hon. member's party is so often willing to expound, people should go into the service in order to serve, not for what they can earn. If they want to serve on a Crown corporation which is serving the public, they should do so because they want to serve and not for the salary they are going to earn. Rest assured the vice-president and members of the board of directors of this Crown corporation will not be walking around with a tin cup. They will be adequately paid. However, there ought to be a limit and a check on growth in order to protect the consumer who would be forced into the monopolistic situation and, I submit, its inherent growth. I commend this amendment to the House and urge that members support it.

I think the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) will concur that the hon. members of the standing joint committee proceeded with great expedition to consider the regulation-making authority in the bill and make recommendations in our report to the House as quickly as possible, and that the exercise was useful and helped us to get a grip on the whole issue as to what was involved in the regulation-making authority the government was requesting.
What would be the implications of giving the government that authority? As the Chair is aware, and as the Postmaster General will be aware, the committee, in many instances, has brought to the attention of Parliament the fact that often bills are passed by Parliament which give the government regulation-making authority beyond that which is needed, and beyond that which has ever been justified to Parliament. We recognize it is a role for regulations to play, that the government must ask Parliament for authority to operate by regulation from time to time. However, we should recognize that whenever the government asks for that authority, it is asking for discretion to change law on the basis of delegated legislation, to change the law in a way which may affect the rights and privileges and incomes of Canadians.
What we find here is yet another clause where the Postmaster General is asking that the government be given the right to pass regulations. In this instance it would affect the ability of the Post Office to delay mail. The members of the standing joint committee recognize the fact that in some instances there is justification for withholding mail and not allowing it to go through. The Postmaster General was kind enough, when he was before the committee, to give explanations as to why he felt it was necessary that power be given to the Post Office to hold and not deliver mail in some instances. The committee considered the arguments of the Postmaster General and found them persuasive. It found that there was justification for holding and not delivering mail in some instances. However, it felt that the regulation-making authorities being asked for by the Postmaster General were far too broad, that he was asking for regulation-making authority which was not sufficiently justified to Parliament, and that all of the purposes for which he was asking authority to hold mail and not to deliver it could be accomplished by being more specific in the bill itself. Consequently, when the committee made its report to Parliament, paragraph 11 of that report dealt with this particular issue. It is a brief paragraph, and I think it would be useful to put it into the record. It reads as follows:
Paragraph (m) of Clause 17(1) contains a very large and vague grant of enabling power permitting the making of regulations 'providing for the holding of mail by the Corporation at the request of the sender or addressee thereof-
The following words are in italics in our report:
-or in any other circumstances specified in the regulations'. The underlined words (the italicized words) carry with them the potential for the holding of mail for purposes not now envisaged. The reason for this inclusion was explained to your committee as being, first, to accommodate bulk mailers who mail in advance, which would seem to be a matter covered by the first part of the
paragraph and, secondly, to cope with situations in which, because of strikes, insurrection or war, overseas mail is 'embargoed'. Your committee recommends that the underlined words be deleted and that some such words as the following be added:
'or at the request of the government of any country, or any independent postal
authority in the event of industrial disputes, insurrection or war.'
If the minister agrees with the amendment our committee has proposed, it would cover all of those instances where the Postmaster General has indicated he has given any justification to Parliament or to our committee for a decision by the Post Office to not deliver mail.
As I indicated previously, the committee felt that in some instances, if, indeed, there was a war or insurrection or postal disruption in another country, and if that country would prefer, because of the chaos, that mail be held until order be restored, that it is appropriate. If bulk mailers were to deliver large quantities of mail to the post office and ask that it be held and not delivered until a certain day, that would be absolutely appropriate also. That is simply a matter of providing service to a customer and ensuring that the needs of customers are met.
The committee had no complaints about that whatsoever. Our concern came from the fact that the government was asking for the authority to make regulations which went well beyond the scope of any justification ever given to Parliament. What we have stressed in report after report is that where the government asks for the authority to make regulations and where Parliament is delegating that authority to the executive and to the government, the government has the responsibility to first justify to Parliament the need for that regulation-making authority. If it can justify it, so be it. If it can justify only a portion of that authority, and if it is possible to spell out, in the wording of an amendment or specific clause or paragraph of a bill, exactly what it is that the government needs the authority for, so be it.
We believe the regulation-making authority held by the government, which is given by Parliament and which is out of the hands of Parliament, by and large, after it is given to the government, should be as constrained as possible. It should have been first justified and explained to Parliament and the Canadian people. Only that power and that regulation-making authority which has previously been justified to Parliament should be granted to the government.
As the committee report pointed out, the amendment which we have proposed here today would cover all of those instances which the Postmaster General proposed to our committee as justification for the withholding of mail.
If the government had other concerns as well, and if the Postmaster General had raised other concerns which could have been justified, we would have been prepared to see them also written into the bill in an explicit way, but we have tried to cover all those areas mentioned by the Postmaster General as being appropriate areas for the government to have the authority not to deliver mail which has been put into the system.

However, there is nothing in the clause, as it now stands, which requires that the direction, once having been given, must be made public.
When Clause 20 was in front of the committee before Christmas, I argued strenuously that directions were legitimate but that they ought not to be kept secret. On the basis of that I moved an amendment in committee which would have required, after a direction is given, that it be then properly laid before Parliament where it could be examined by members of Parliament and the public.
At the time the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) was not disposed to accept that amendment and, as a consequence, it was defeated. Since then I have made it clear on a number of occasions in public statements that my party viewed the secret aspect of these directions very seriously and that we hoped, as soon as the government realized the degree of seriousness with which we view this particular problem, there might be some disposition on the part of the government to rethink its position taken in committee.
The Postmaster General knows I pointed out that the problem with secret directions is that management, as a consequence of a direction, may very well have to make a management decision which might be quite inexplicable, unless it was made clear that the decision was being made as a consequence of the direct intervention of the Government of Canada.
Those members of the House who concern themselves with the labour relations aspect of the Post Office ought to be very aware that unions negotiating with the management of the Post Office ought not to feel that somewhere behind the curtain secret directions are being given to management by government which could affect negotiations.

For example, there is an automatic reference to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.

That is one of the things this Parliament has provided the Auditor General, that", 'April 8, 1981
Canada Post Corporation Act
is, the right of access to essential information. The bill does not provide for the qualified privilege of an auditor's report and statements.

speechtext:
Motion No. 9
That Bill C-42, an act to establish the Canada Post Corporation, to repeal the Post Office Act and other related acts and to make related amendments to other acts, be amended by deleting clause 31 and substituting the following therefor: "31. The accounts and financial transactions of the Corporation shall be
audited annually by the Auditor General."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a long clause which provides that the corporation will have two auditors. A number of other clauses provide how they shall work. It is the position of this party that the Auditor General of Canada, who is developing a comprehensive system of auditing Crown corporations in order to protect the public interest and to make the disclosure that parliamentarians and the whole country require, should audit the corporation. We do not need companies such as Touche Ross or Coopers & Lybrand and the like to audit the postal
corporation at government expense. This corporation is not in real competition with other private corporations. Its purpose, presumably is to facilitate the government's mandate to deliver the mail. This department of government is to become a corporation but it will not be a corporation like Air Canada or Canadian National Railways. By its very nature it is subject to directive by governor in council, to ministerial directive; indeed, almost everything it does, including setting postal rates, is subject to direction by the governor in council. That being the case it is essential that Parliament's auditor conduct the audit of the corporation. I could say a great deal about the cost of private auditing. Parliament's auditor should do the work in accordance with the kind of report required by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. This corporation will be something like Statistics Canada or Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and it should be audited in the same fashion. To suggest that the Auditor General is not capable is to cast a slur on him; that just is not so.
This corporation must report to Parliament in the manner in which Parliament is accustomed to receiving reports. A comprehensive audit should be carried out and the auditing practices of the Auditor General of Canada should be followed year after year. The audit should not be farmed out to one auditing company or another. The way that the corporation operates, its profitability and the use of money Parliament from time to time may need to vote in the estimates to support its activities, should be part of Parliament's auditing practice. Indeed, the Comptroller General should be involved and the report of the Auditor General should come before the committees of Parliament.
We are not happy with the way the post office has operated in the past and so we are about to experiment with a new postal corporation. There are many ways of going about this and of doing audit. The hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) pointed out an instance where an auditing company put a great qualification on the balance sheet of de Havilland aircraft. That was a private audit. But where a qualification is required we think that Auditor General of Canada should explain the matter. Members of Parliament cannot ask a private auditing company to explain the details of the financial requirements of the corporation if they are not empowered to do so by a committee of the House. How are they to find out where the money is being spent and how effective and efficient the corporation is? It is our position that the Auditor General of Canada should audit this corporation and that motion No. 9 should be adopted.
